chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Abdullah ibn Sa'id al-Askari narrated to us, saying: My uncle informed me, saying: Abu Ishaq informed us, saying: Tha'laba dictated to us the hours of the night: Al-Ghasq, Al-Fahme, Al-Eshwa, Al-Huda, Al-Jonh, Al-Hazia, Al-Faqd, Al-Aqr, Al-Zulfa, Al-Sahra, and Al-Bahra; and the hours of the day: Al-Rad, Al-Shuruq, Al-Matu, Al-Tarhil, Al-Dakuk, Al-Januh, Al-Hajeer, Al-Zahira, Al-Aseel, and Al-Tifl.
ai.seo_question: What are the traditional Arabic names for the hours of the night and day?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Khisal* preserves the pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabic lexicon for dividing the day and night into twelve distinct temporal segments, as transmitted by the scholar Tha'laba. These specific terms, such as *al-Fahma* (deep night) and *al-Zulfah* (late night), provide essential linguistic and jurisprudential context for understanding the precise timing of *Salat* and other devotional acts in Shia tradition. The detailed enumeration reflects the Islamic emphasis on structuring daily life around divine remembrance and natural cycles.
